questions.q: Which of these best captures the 'sharper' definition of metadata given in this lesson?
options: What makes data findable, understandable, and trustworthy without opening it first
A backup copy of the data stored in a different system
Any data that is more than one year old
The physical storage format a database uses on disk
questions.explain: The lesson's sharper definition moves past 'data about data' to the functional payoff: metadata lets you decide whether to use something before you have to open and inspect it.

questions.q: In the library card catalog analogy, what does the card represent?
options: The book itself
Metadata about the book — not the book's actual content
A duplicate copy of the book kept in a second location
The library's budget records
questions.explain: The card lists title, author, subject, and shelf location — structured facts about the book that let you decide whether to go get it, without pulling every book off the shelf.

questions.q: Which of these is given as an everyday example of metadata in this lesson?
options: A file's 'Date Modified' column in a file explorer
The actual text written inside a document
A phone call between two colleagues
A handwritten note with no file system record
questions.explain: Date Modified is technical metadata generated automatically by the file system — it describes the file without being the file's content.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what kind of problem is 'we have the data somewhere, nobody knows where' usually?
options: A metadata problem, not a data problem
A hardware storage capacity problem
A network bandwidth problem
An encryption key management problem
questions.explain: The data often exists; what's missing is the metadata (name, description, owner, location) that would let someone find and trust it without manually searching every system.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does Metadata Management & Business Glossary exist as its own course rather than being folded into Data Governance Foundations?
options: Because metadata is the infrastructure governance roles, policies, and lineage actually run on, and deserves its own depth
Because metadata has nothing to do with data governance
Because this course replaces Data Governance Foundations entirely
Because metadata is only relevant to software engineers, not governance practitioners
questions.explain: You can't assign a data owner to an unfindable dataset, enforce a naming standard with nowhere to record it, or build lineage without metadata describing what systems produce — this course builds that underlying infrastructure in depth.
